PMC1026: Pharmaceutical Physiology

Regulation of Transcription
Dr Dan Corbett

media.webLabel: Open slide 1 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 2
pages.text:
Why is this Important?
• So far, we’ve considered processes like transcription and translation in a very basic
  way – even though it might not seem like it!
• Genes are present in our DNA - these are transcribed and then translated
• BUT – you have different cells, which do different things…
• …and those different cells can do different things at different times, based on the situation
  they’re in!
• Whilst most of our cells will contain a full set of our DNA, they don’t all use all of this
  information for their function
• Transcription is regulated in cells, with the transcription of particular genes happening at
  particular times
• We often refer to this as the genes being “switched on” when the protein they code for is
  needed – this is a simplification!
• Understanding this allows us to learn more about how our cells work, how their function is
  controlled, and ultimately, to design drugs which can target this process, “switching”
  genes on or off!

media.webLabel: Open slide 2 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 3
pages.text:
Regulation of Transcription

Part 1. The Basics

media.webLabel: Open slide 3 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 4
pages.text:
Why is Transcription Regulated?
• The transcription of genes controls which proteins are produced in a
  cell
• If the gene for a protein is transcribed, it can then be translated into
  that protein
• So, regulating transcription is the way in which a cell regulates the
  proteins that it produces and contains
• As we’ve mentioned, different cells will have different protein
  “profiles” depending on what they do, and the situation that they’re in
• ”Regulated” does not mean “stopped” – it simply means that each
  gene in a cell is switched on or off, depending on need
• This allows our cells to adapt and respond to changing conditions –
  very useful!

media.webLabel: Open slide 4 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 5
pages.jumpLabel: Switching Genes on and Off - Examples
pages.text:
Switching Genes on and Off - Examples
• Just had a meal? Cells in your pancreas will see the gene for
  insulin being switched on, so that blood glucose levels can be
  better managed
• Picked up an infection? Genes in immune system cells will be
  switched on to produce proteins which help to fight the pathogen
• Taken a medication? Genes in your liver cells will be switched on,
  producing proteins which will break that drug down, helping to
  remove it from your body
• Time to go to bed? Changes in environmental conditions (like
  darkness) can activate genes that help regulate your sleep-wake
  cycle, assisting you in falling asleep

media.webLabel: Open slide 5 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 6
pages.text:
“Always On” Genes
• Whilst some genes are regulated up or down depending on need/conditions,
  there are some proteins that we need all the time
• Need a protein all the time? Then the gene needs to be switched on all the
  time!
• We refer to these genes as being constitutive:
   • Genes which are responsible for making RNA polymerase, tRNA and
     ribosomes
   • The genes which make the proteins which form key cell structures – actin
     and tubulin for example (remember these?)
   • Genes for the proteins which help to make energy in the cell, and help to
     clean the cell up
   • Genes which allow for DNA replication and repair – more on that in
     another lecture!

media.webLabel: Open slide 6 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 7
pages.jumpLabel: Knowing this is important – the fundamentals of the
pages.text:
Knowing this is important – the fundamentals of the
regulation of gene transcription is that these processes
will take place at certain times, under certain conditions!

  These conditions will bring about various biochemical
actions at the DNA-level, switching genes on or off as the
                      need arises!

 Our genome doesn’t stay still – it’s an always-changing
system that adjusts its output based on the needs of the
cell, the tissues those cells make, and the organism as a
     whole, as well as external environmental factors!

media.webLabel: Open slide 7 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 8
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · A dial on the transcript count
pages.text:
One Lock, Many Keys
• The regulation of gene transcription is complex!
• We can think of it as an on/off switch generally, but in reality, there are a lot
  of switches which work together to cause a gene to be transcribed – or
  not…
• …and which control the amount of transcription of a gene, leading to more
  or less protein being made!
• To make things even more complicated, some of the parts that we’re
  interested in are located on the DNA itself…
• …and others are molecules which are floating around the cell, and which
  can make their way to the DNA and cause an effect on how much a certain
  gene is transcribed
• These parts will work together to control transcription to a very high level!
• Let’s think more about these!

media.webLabel: Open slide 8 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: A dial on the transcript count
practice.prompt: Two cell samples both transcribe a gene. In one, many more transcripts are made over the same time. Does this comparison fit regulation, even though transcription occurs in both cells? Explain.
practice.answer: Yes. Regulation can adjust the amount of transcription. The lower count does not require the gene to be completely switched off.

pages.title: Slide 9
pages.text:
Regulation of Transcription

Part 2. Regulation at the DNA

media.webLabel: Open slide 9 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 10
pages.text:
Remember that “Junk” DNA?
• …we should already know that it’s definitely not “junk” – for a range
  of reasons!
• In this case, our DNA contains portions which don’t code for a
  protein, but instead, act as docking sites for pre-existing proteins
• Once they bind to their docking site, these proteins have an effect on
  the transcription of the gene
• These docking sites on the DNA can be close to the gene we’re
  interested in, or quite far away from it – but they’ll all have a say in
  how that gene is transcribed!
• It’s important to remember that these sequences are located within
  the same DNA molecule which they’re helping to control!

media.webLabel: Open slide 10 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 11
pages.text:
The Promoter



• We’ve heard about this already
• It’s located quite close to the start of the gene which is being transcribed
• It’s found at the start of all protein-coding genes
• It acts as the start site for transcription, thus controlling if a gene is transcribed at all!
• Because of this, we refer to the promoter as the basal promoter – it’ll allow the baseline
  level of transcription on its own
• It’s where RNA polymerase binds – and we know what this does!
• BUT - RNA doesn’t just bind directly to DNA itself, without any help

media.webLabel: Open slide 11 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 12
pages.text:
The Promoter - Structure
• This part of the DNA sequence is highly conserved – we’ll see it in
  an unchanged state at the start of most of our protein coding genes,
  and in the genes of lots of other organisms too!
• This section contains the TATA box – called this because it generally
  contains this sequence of nucleotides: TATAAA – but this can vary a
  little!
• This is where TATA binding protein binds – this is one of the
  proteins which will help RNA polymerase to bind to the promoter!
• The binding of TATA binding protein then allows other proteins to
  attach, which can further help RNA polymerase out, getting it into the
  right location to do its job!
• These proteins are called transcription factors!

media.webLabel: Open slide 12 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 13
pages.text:
Promoter Proximal Elements
• So, the promoter is just one piece of the puzzle!
• It’s essential for the basic machinery of transcription to work
• Promoter proximal (beside) elements allow for fine-tuned
  regulation
• They provide specific binding sites for transcription factors, which
  can either enhance or repress the transcription process
• External proteins and other substances can bind to these too –
  either starting or stopping transcription based on the environment
• These elements are also involved in helping genes to be
  transcribed only in the cells that need those genes - they’ll be
  specific for chemicals which are produced in those cells only!

pages.title: Slide 15
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · Two views of the same DNA
pages.text:
Getting Further Away and More
Complicated!
• In addition to the promoter and promoter-proximal elements, there
  are other regions of DNA which can affect how transcription happens
• These are called silencers and enhancers…
• …and they act as attachment sites for repressor and activator
  proteins
• They can be located before the gene being transcribed on the DNA
  strand, after it, or even within it!
• The looping of DNA allows these regions, which can be far away
  from the gene, to come into contact with the complexes around the
  transcription start site – this is assisted by looping proteins
• Gene transcription is a very three-dimensional process!

media.webLabel: Open slide 15 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Two views of the same DNA
practice.prompt: On a flat sequence diagram a regulatory site appears far from a promoter. In the three-dimensional drawing, their associated proteins sit together. How can the two drawings be consistent?
practice.answer: The intervening DNA can form a loop. Distance along the sequence can be large even when folding brings the regulatory region close to the promoter in space.

pages.title: Slide 16
pages.text:
The DNA bends into a loop. Activators bound at a distant enhancer lie close to transcription factors, mediator proteins and RNA polymerase at the promoter.

Activators and Repressors

media.webLabel: Open slide 16 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 17
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · Label the parts of a switch
pages.text:
Activators and Repressors
• What this all means is that:
    • An activator protein bound to an enhancer section of DNA
      will INCREASE the transcription of the gene in question
    • A repressor protein bound to a silencer section of DNA will
      DECREASE the amount of transcription of the gene in
      question
• There are lots of ways in which these proteins will cause their
  effects – it’s complicated!
• We can also see competition between activators and
  repressors – normally, this all keeps transcription of a gene nice
  and balanced

media.webLabel: Open slide 17 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Label the parts of a switch
practice.prompt: A drawing shows a protein attached to a DNA region. The caption says this combination increases transcription of a nearby gene. Give the names of the DNA site and its protein partner in this example.
practice.answer: The DNA region is an enhancer. Its bound protein is an activator. Naming which is DNA and which is protein makes the drawing interpretable.

pages.title: Slide 18
pages.text:
The Importance of Transcription
Factors
• So far, we’ve talked about all these regions on the DNA that
  help to control transcription
• But these sections of DNA don’t work alone – they simply
  act as attachment sites for transcription factors, which
  then go on to do the job in question, increasing or
  decreasing transcription!
• With that in mind, we need to think a little about where
  those transcription factors come from!
• But first…

media.webLabel: Open slide 18 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 19
pages.text:
Other Approaches to Regulate
Transcription
• In addition to the interaction of various proteins with DNA sites
  around the gene, there are other chemical processes which
  can affect levels of gene transcription
• These processes will happen in response to various
  environmental factors!
• DNA methylation and demethylation:
    • Methyl groups are added to or removed from some of the
      adenine and cytosine bases in the DNA at the promoter site
    • Methylated = reduces transcription factor binding and can
      wrap DNA more tightly = transcription reduced
    • Demethylated = the opposite = transcription enhanced

media.webLabel: Open slide 19 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 20
pages.text:
Other Approaches to Regulate
Transcription
• In addition to the interaction of various proteins with DNA sites
  around the gene, there are other chemical processes which
  can affect levels of gene transcription
• These processes will happen in response to various
  environmental factors!
• Histone acetylation and deacetylation
    • Histone proteins assist with the coiling of DNA
    • Addition of acetyl groups to histone proteins (acetylation)
      unwinds DNA and promotes gene transcription
    • Deacetylation does the opposite

media.webLabel: Open slide 20 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 21
pages.text:
Regulation of Transcription

Part 3. The Importance of
Transcription Factors

media.webLabel: Open slide 21 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 22
pages.text:
Transcription Factors are Important!

• So far, we know that transcription factors are proteins
  which will bind to specific DNA sequences
• When this happens, they’ll influence the transcription of
  the gene
• Those effects will be related to the part of the DNA that
  they bind to, and their own structure and function
• Understanding how these proteins work, and when they
  work is key to understanding how transcription is
  regulated!

media.webLabel: Open slide 22 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 23
pages.text:
Different Cells, Different Factors

• We know that different cells do different things at
  different times, based on the situation they’re in!
• To do this, different cells possess different sets of
  transcription factors
• Those transcription factors are involved in the
  expression of different genes
• This all explains how different cells can express
  different genes, and why not all cells express all genes
  – or even just the same ones from a shorter list!

media.webLabel: Open slide 23 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Two cell types
practice.prompt: Two cell types contain a particular gene. One expresses it much more strongly under the conditions shown. What difference between the cells does this lecture suggest checking before assuming their DNA differs?
practice.answer: Their sets of transcription factors can differ. Which factors are present helps determine which genes are transcribed in each cell type.

pages.title: Slide 24
pages.text:
Regulation of Transcription Factors

• Much like a lot of genes, transcription factors aren’t
  turned on all the time either
• If they were, they’d all attach to their binding sites, all try
  and do their own jobs, and we’d have chaos!
• So, we have layers of regulation – the activation of
  transcription factors is regulated, which in turn allows
  them to regulate transcription!
• Transcription factors are regulated in a range of different
  ways

media.webLabel: Open slide 24 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 25
pages.text:
Regulation of Transcription Factors –
How?
• Transcription factors can be activated/deactivated by:
   • Post-translational modification – chemical modification of
     the transcription factor protein somewhere in the cell
   • The binding of ligands – attachment of another substance
     to the protein causing a change in its conformation
   • Environmental conditions – which then change the
     conformation of the protein
   • Their forced localisation – the protein might already be
     active, but a signal is needed to allow it to travel to the
     nucleus of the cell, rather than the signal activating or
     deactivating the protein directly!
   • …and other things too!

Regulation of Transcription

Part 4. Regulation of Transcription –
Who Cares?

media.webLabel: Open slide 27 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 28
pages.jumpLabel: Who Cares about the Regulation of
pages.text:
Who Cares about the Regulation of
Transcription?
• Well, we do!
• Knowing about these processes is important – firstly, because we need to
  know how these things work normally, in health
• But, we also need to understand how these things can go wrong, because
  this is the basis of many diseases
• Conditions can be caused by the:
   • Overexpression of transcription factors
   • Underexpression of transcription factors
   • Transcription factor mutation and dysfunction
• …all of which can lead to the transcription/non-transcription of genes
  which our cells need/don’t need to remain healthy!

media.webLabel: Open slide 28 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 29
pages.text:
Disease Examples
• Many cancers can be caused by the overactivity of
  transcription factors which then cause the over-transcription of
  lots of genes which cause cells to divide and multiply
• Overactivation of the NF-κB transcription factor can lead to the
  over-transcription of genes which are involved in inflammation,
  leading to prolonged inflammation and damage of joints in
  rheumatoid arthritis
• Huntington’s disease can be caused by the overexpression of
  a repressor in nerve cells – this reduces the transcription of
  important genes in those nerve cells, leading to the
  development of this condition

media.webLabel: Open slide 29 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 30
pages.text:
Transcription Regulation as a
Treatment Target
• Now that we know about the regulation of transcription and where it
  can go wrong, we’ve got a good set of tools to work with
• These tools can help us to identify how diseases work
• Once we’ve got that worked out, and identified the transcription
  factor which is involved, we’ve now got a target which we can aim
  for to treat the condition
• Approaches could include:
    • Directly interacting with the transcription factor
    • Doing things to increase or reduce its activity
    • Doing something else which might affect how these factors work
      to regulate transcription!

media.webLabel: Open slide 30 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 31
pages.text:
Treatment Target Examples
• Tamoxifen binds to the estrogen receptor, stopping its
  activation – this prevents it causing the transcription of genes
  which cause the replication and division of cells in breast
  cancer
• Cyclosporine prevents the activation of T-cells by inactivating
  proteins which help to make NF-AT, which is a transcription
  factor that causes the transcription of activating genes in T-cells
  – why might this be a useful treatment?
• Actinomycin binds directly to DNA, sticking into the middle of
  G-C base pairs, including those at the promoter – this stops
  the attachment of RNA polymerase, and prevents
  transcription from getting started!

media.webLabel: Open slide 31 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 32
pages.text:
To Sum Up…
• We’ve now taken our basic knowledge of the structure of DNA
  and genes, and their transcription, and turned this into
  knowledge which is applicable to the design of drug therapies
• We now know that transcription is very highly-regulated in a
  healthy state, which in turn makes sure that all our cells are
  tightly controlled, and produce the substances that they need
• Knowing all of this allows us to know of all the ways that things
  could go wrong – this is the basis of a huge number of diseases
• But, if we know about what the diseases do, and how this
  affects gene transcription, we have a lot of the information we
  need to make a drug to counteract the problem!

media.webLabel: Open slide 32 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 33
pages.text:
Next Time…

• Now that we know what our genes are like, how they’re
  structured, and what they do, it’s important to think
  about how we get our hands on these genes
• To do this, we inherit them from the people who made
  us – our parents!
• We’ll think about how we inherit genetic material, and
  consider how this can go wrong, which in turn can lead
  to the emergence of lots of diseases and conditions
